title: The Firmament and the Shape of the World
lead: How the Bible pictures the world. God spreads out the sky like a tent or hammers it out like metal. There are waters above it. The earth stands on bases and pillars, under the round line of the horizon. Christians read this picture in several ways, set out below. On every reading the point is the same: God made it all, and nothing holds it up but him.

sections.h: The dome and the waters above
sections.b:
On the second day God makes a raqia'. The Plain English Translation calls it a "dome." God "divided the waters under the dome from the waters above the dome" (Genesis 1:7). The related verb raqa' means to hammer or beat out. It is used for gold beaten into thin plates (Exodus 39:3). It is also used for bronze censers beaten into a cover for the altar (Numbers 16:39). Elihu asks Job whether he can "join him in hammering out the skies, / hard as a mirror cast from metal" (Job 37:18).

The Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) has stereōma, "something firm." Jerome's Latin has firmamentum, and that gave the KJV its word "firmament." A psalm calls on "you waters over the heavens" to praise God (Psalm 148:4). The flood comes when "the windows of the sky" open (Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:2). Ezekiel sees a dome "shining like awesome ice" above the living creatures (Ezekiel 1:22). Yet the Bible also pictures the sky as cloth. God "stretches the heavens out like a thin veil" (Isaiah 40:22). He spreads them "like a tent curtain" (Psalm 104:2).

sections.h: Bases, pillars, and an earth hung on nothing
sections.b:
Hannah sings, "The earth's pillars belong to the LORD, / and he has set the world on them" (1 Samuel 2:8). God says, "I myself have made its pillars firm" (Psalm 75:3). He asks Job, "Into what were its bases sunk? / Who set down its corner stone" (Job 38:6). When God shakes the world, "the pillars under it shudder" (Job 9:6). But Job also says, "on nothing at all he hangs the earth" (Job 26:7). The Hebrew belimah means "without anything," and the Greek has "on nothing."

"He is seated high over the circle of the earth" (Isaiah 40:22). The Hebrew chug is a circle drawn on a surface. The same word is used when God "carved a circle on the surface of the deep" (Proverbs 8:27). A verb from the same root is used when he "traced a ring across the surface of the waters" (Job 26:10). The Greek has gyros, "a ring." Ray Comfort reads the verse as saying that "the earth is round." Isaiah knew a word for a ball, dur (Isaiah 22:18), and does not use it here. On either reading, the verse pictures God enthroned high above the earth. In the same way, "the four corners of the earth" (Revelation 7:1; Isaiah 11:12) means "everywhere." English speakers still say "the four corners of the globe."

sections.b:
Each reading below is held by Christians who take the Bible as God's word. Each is given in its own strongest form.

Real waters above (young-earth creation). Many young-earth creationists read the waters above as real water. In The Genesis Flood (1961), John Whitcomb and Henry Morris took the "expanse" as the troposphere, the lowest layer of the air. Above it they placed "a pre-flood canopy of waters." That canopy, they argued, gave "an adequate source for the waters of a universal flood" (compare Genesis 7:11). Later, Russell Humphreys of the Institute for Creation Research placed the waters above at the outer edge of the universe.

Water in the sky (old-earth creation). Hugh Ross of Reasons to Believe, a leading progressive creationist, also reads the raqia' as an expanse. He calls Genesis 1:6–8 "a brief comment" on water above the earth's surface "in the troposphere" and water below "in the oceans and lakes." He notes that God named the dome "Sky" (Genesis 1:8). In his view, the translation "dome" rests on a "myth" about what ancient peoples believed. Randall Younker and Richard Davidson of Andrews University make the same case in "The Myth of the Solid Heavenly Dome" (2011).

The world as it looks. Calvin read raqia' as "expanse" and took the waters above to be the clouds. He wrote that in Genesis 1 "nothing is here treated of but the visible form of the world." "He who would learn astronomy, and other recondite arts, let him go elsewhere." Long before him, Basil the Great said the firmament "is not in reality a firm and solid substance." Yet he also insisted that "by water water is meant," against those who made the waters a picture of spiritual powers (Hexaemeron 3). Today Vern Poythress (Interpreting Eden, 2019) reads the waters above as the water in clouds. He calls the passage "a description of appearances," not a theory of the sky. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978, Article XIII) says the Bible's truth is not undone by "observational descriptions of nature."

An ancient picture God spoke within. Paul Seely argues that the raqia' "was originally conceived of as being solid." He shows that most ancient readers took it that way. Origen called the firmament "without doubt firm and solid." Augustine said the name shows "that it is solid and that it constitutes an impassable boundary between the waters above and the waters below." Jewish teachers even tried to work out how thick it was (Genesis Rabbah 4:5). Martin Luther wrote that the stars "are fastened to the firmament like globes of fire." Of "the waters above the heavens" he said, "we must believe them rather than wickedly deny them" (Lectures on Genesis). The conservative scholar E. J. Young defined raqia' as "that which is hammered, beaten out." Seely also names critical scholars who read it this way: Driver, Gunkel, Skinner, von Rad and Westermann. Seely still calls the verse "infallibly true." Its purpose, he says, is not "to teach us the physical nature of the sky, but to reveal the creator of the sky." He quotes the Reformed theologian B. B. Warfield, who allowed that an inspired writer might "share the ordinary opinions of his day" about "the form of the earth."

Ancient science and a sure message (evolutionary creation). Denis Lamoureux, author of Evolutionary Creation (2008), agrees that the Bible speaks of a solid firmament holding up a heavenly sea. He calls this the "ancient science" of the day. In his view the Holy Spirit came down to the writers' level, as God came down to us in Jesus. So he separates "the incidental ancient science" from "the inerrant message of faith." He also notes that Psalm 148:4, written after the flood, still speaks of "waters over the heavens," which he counts against the canopy view.

A hint of later science. Some readers see knowledge here ahead of its time. Ray Comfort writes that "The Bible proclaims that the earth freely floats in space." He bases this on Job 26:7. Henry Morris wrote, "The Bible is a book of science!" Lamoureux calls this approach "concordism" and argues against it. Readers who see poetry here point out that the same books also speak of pillars and bases (Job 9:6; Job 38:6).

sections.h: Did the church teach a flat earth?
sections.b:
Many people today think the medieval church taught a flat earth. The historian Jeffrey Burton Russell calls this an error. He wrote that "with extraordinary few exceptions no educated person in the history of Western Civilization from the third century B.C. onward believed that the Earth was flat." He traced the story to writers of the 1800s such as John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White.

There were exceptions. Lactantius, writing in the early 300s, mocked those who thought "that the world is round like a ball." He asked whether anyone was "so senseless as to believe that there are men whose footsteps are higher than their heads" (Divine Institutes 3.24). In 1837 William Whewell named him and Cosmas Indicopleustes (Christian Topography, about 548) as Christians who held a flat earth.

Augustine took a middle course. He wrote of the case where "it be supposed or scientifically demonstrated that the world is of a round and spherical form." He did not argue against a round world. What he rejected was the "fable" that people lived on the far side (The City of God 16.9).

The rabbis, too, could learn from outsiders. The sages of Israel and of the nations disagreed about where the sun goes at night. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said the other sages' view "appears to be more accurate than our statement" (Pesachim 94b).

common: The church once taught that the earth was flat.
The word "firmament" comes straight from the Hebrew; in fact it comes from Jerome's Latin firmamentum, which follows the Greek stereōma.
uncommon: Basil the Great taught in the 300s that the firmament "is not in reality a firm and solid substance."
Calvin and Luther differed on the waters above: Calvin took them to be the clouds, while Luther said to believe in them even where we cannot understand them.
